subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A speech opens and closes with the very same phrase, "We will not be moved." Framing a text this way is best described as:
questions.explain: Beginning and ending with the same idea creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: "The letter still lay unopened on the mat, its corner curling in the morning sun." What does the detail of the unopened letter most likely IMPLY?
options: Someone is avoiding or dreading its contents
The character is keen to read it
questions.explain: An unopened, neglected letter implies reluctance or dread rather than eagerness.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a writer SHOWING rather than TELLING emotion?
options: "She bit her nails and glanced at the door again and again."
questions.explain: Describing actions (nail-biting, glancing) lets the reader infer nervousness, which is "showing."

questions.q: When an extract suddenly shifts focus from a wide view of a crowd to one trembling child, this structural technique:
options: Changes the narrator to second person
Narrows the focus to direct the reader's attention
questions.explain: Moving from the general to a single detail is a deliberate narrowing of focus that guides reader attention.

questions.q: "The forest was a cathedral of green." The comparison of the forest to a cathedral mainly creates a sense of:
questions.explain: A cathedral connotes height, quiet and awe, so the metaphor lends the forest grandeur and reverence.

questions.q: "Time is a thief that steals our youth." This describing of time AS a thief is a:
questions.explain: Calling time a thief directly, without "like" or "as," is a metaphor.

questions.q: A writer follows a long, flowing description with the single line: "Everything stopped." Standing alone as its own paragraph, this short sentence creates:
options: A sudden pause and dramatic emphasis
questions.explain: An isolated short sentence after long ones forces a pause and lands with dramatic impact.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the MOOD created by: "The fog pressed against the windows and the house creaked in the dark."?
questions.explain: Fog, darkness and creaking build a tense, eerie atmosphere.

questions.q: What is the reader most likely meant to FEEL from: "The orphan watched the other children open their gifts, his own hands empty"?
questions.explain: The image of the empty-handed orphan beside happy children is designed to evoke sympathy.

questions.q: An extract begins in the middle of a chase with no introduction of who is running or why. This opening technique is designed to:
options: Explain the whole plot at once
Plunge the reader straight into the action and create immediacy
Bore the reader before the action
questions.explain: Starting mid-action (in medias res) creates immediacy and draws the reader in at once.

questions.q: A third-person narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character is described as:
questions.explain: An omniscient narrator has access to all characters' inner thoughts and the wider story.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the ATMOSPHERE in "Sunlight spilled across the kitchen and the kettle hummed a cheerful tune"?
questions.explain: Sunlight, a humming kettle and a "cheerful" tune build a warm, comforting atmosphere.

questions.q: A dove is used throughout a text to represent peace. Using an object to stand for an idea is:
questions.explain: An object standing for a larger idea (a dove for peace) is symbolism.

questions.q: A first-person narrator insists "I did nothing wrong" while describing clearly cruel behaviour. This narrator is best described as:
questions.explain: When the narrator's account conflicts with the evidence, they are an unreliable narrator.

questions.q: A narrator describes events plainly with no access to anyone's thoughts, simply reporting what is seen and heard. This perspective is best called:
questions.explain: Reporting only observable action without inner thoughts is an objective third-person perspective.

questions.q: "His coat was patched and his shoes had holes, but he held his head high." What does this most strongly imply about the character?
questions.explain: The contrast between worn clothes and a high-held head implies pride and dignity despite hardship.

questions.q: "The wind whispered through the trees." Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Giving the wind the human ability to "whisper" is personification.

questions.q: Words such as "however," "meanwhile" and "firstly" that signal the direction of a text are:
questions.explain: Connectives that guide the reader through a text are discourse markers.

questions.q: "Bitter sweet," "deafening silence" and "living dead" are examples of:
questions.explain: Two contradictory words placed together form an oxymoron.

questions.q: "She laughed, but her eyes stayed cold." The contrast in this sentence most strongly suggests her laughter is:
options: Insincere or hiding her true feelings
questions.explain: Warm laughter set against cold eyes implies the laughter is false and conceals real feeling.

questions.q: "The thunder grumbled and the rain drummed on the roof." Which TWO techniques are combined here?
questions.explain: "Grumbled" personifies the thunder while "drummed" imitates sound (onomatopoeia).

questions.q: "The classroom was a zoo." This direct comparison without "like" or "as" is a:
questions.explain: Stating one thing IS another is a metaphor.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Language (J351) specification; Paper 2 Exploring Effects And Impact
